title: erm(46) copy number determines macrolide resistance in Rhodococcus equi.
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
abstract: To develop a multiplex real-time PCR assay for simultaneous detection of Rhodococcus equi (choE), virulence (vapA), and macrolide-resistance determinants (erm[46], erm[51]), and evaluate their clinical and temporal trends. Clinical R equi isolates (n = 229) obtained from the Hagyard Equine Medical Institute laboratory were collected sequentially over a 3-year surveillance period (2021 to 2023) from 14 states and underwent broth microdilution susceptibility testing. A cohort of 214 isolates with high-quality DNA was characterized using quantitative PCR. Geographic distribution, seasonal trends, and genotypic-phenotypic concordance were evaluated. The multiplex PCR assay demonstrated 100% analytical specificity. The virulence gene vapA was present in 94.4% (202 of 214) of isolates. The macrolide resistance determinant erm(46) was highly prevalent at 62.6% (134 of 214), showing a significant seasonal increase during July to December periods at 76.6% (vs 58.2% in January to June). Crucially, erm(51) was detected in a single isolate (0.5%), representing its first recorded clinical identification in R equi. Unstratified genotypic-phenotypic agreement for macrolides was fair (κ = 0.22 to 0.25). However, stratification by genomic copy number revealed near-perfect concordance (κ ≥ 0.97) exclusively among isolates harboring > 50,000 target copies. Alternative agents (gentamicin, ceftiofur, minocycline, doxycycline) maintained 97% to 100% susceptibility, regardless of erm(46) status. While erm(46) is widely distributed across R equi-endemic farms, actual phenotypic resistance expression is strongly copy-number dependent. The clinical emergence of erm(51) expands the known resistome of this pathogen. Incorporating quantitative molecular screening into routine R equi diagnostics provides crucial real-time therapeutic guidance, supporting precision medicine and targeted antimicrobial stewardship on endemic equine farms.

title: Auscultation for pre-exercise screening in the horse.
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
abstract: To describe the highlights of cardiac auscultation of the equine athlete in the context of pre-exercise screening for cardiac adverse event prevention. Horses. Tutorial description. Description of the highlights of cardiac auscultation of the equine athlete in the context of pre-exercise screening for cardiac adverse event and exercise-associated sudden death prevention. Cardiac adverse events and exercise-associated deaths are problems that affect horses' health, riders' safety, and the public perception of welfare during equestrian sports. Screening before participation in sports has helped decrease the incidence of sudden death in humans. We believe auscultation may be a high-yield, low-cost strategy to improve equine welfare and a key component of a prevention program for exercise-associated sudden death in equine athletes. What we describe here highlights that an irregularly irregular rhythm is atrial fibrillation until proven otherwise and is the main target of pre-exercise auscultation. Concerning murmurs are the second target; multiple examples of audio, video, and electrocardiograms are shown.

title: Infracyanine green photodynamic therapy provides short-term disease control, but recurrence is common in equine immune-mediated keratitis.
abstract: To evaluate long-term clinical outcomes, recurrence rates, and complications following photodynamic therapy (PDT) in horses with immune-mediated keratitis. Medical records of horses treated with PDT at the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences Equine Clinic from May 2018 through October 2025 were reviewed retrospectively. Eyes with a clinical diagnosis of recurrent immune-mediated keratitis that had responded to immunosuppressive therapy and been subjected to PDT therapy were included. Infracyanine green was injected intrastromally, followed by irradiation with an 810-nm diode laser. Recurrence, postoperative complications, and follow-up duration were recorded. Recurrence-free survival was estimated using Kaplan-Meier analysis, and associations with recurrence were explored. 30 eyes from 28 horses were included. Recurrence occurred in 18 of 30 eyes (60.0%); 12 of 30 (40.0%) remained recurrence-free without medication at final follow-up (median, 1,849 days). Recurrence-free survival was 83.1% at 1 year (95% CI, 64.0% to 92.6%) and 49.8% at 2 years (95% CI, 30.2% to 66.6%); median recurrence-free time was 693 days. Postoperative epithelial defects occurred in 22 of 30 eyes (73.3%), and secondary bacterial ulcerative keratitis developed in 4 of 30 (13.3%); all ulcers healed after adjusted treatment. No clear associations between evaluated variables and recurrence were detected. PDT provided medication-free disease control in some eyes, particularly during the first postoperative year, but recurrence was common with longer follow-up. Epithelial defects were frequent, although all resolved without major sequelae. PDT may be useful when prolonged topical treatment is impractical; repeated early fluorescein staining and long-term surveillance are recommended.

title: Intravenous regional limb perfusion techniques in the anesthetized foal.
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
abstract: To provide a video tutorial on how to perform IV regional limb perfusion (IVRLP) using the cephalic or saphenous vein in anesthetized foals. Foals from neonatal to weaning age not amenable to standing, sedated procedures. A pneumatic or wide-rubber tourniquet is applied around the proximal antebrachium or gaskin. The IVRLP dose of desired antimicrobial is diluted with physiologic saline to 30 mL of total volume. A 23-gauge winged infusion set or 22-gauge, 1-inch IV catheter is inserted into either the cephalic or saphenous vein distal to the tourniquet, and the entire perfusate volume is administered slowly by hand or with a syringe pump. The needle or catheter is removed, a pressure bandage applied over the venipuncture site, and the tourniquet left in place for a minimum of 20 minutes and up to 30 minutes. When IVRLP is administered in conjunction with systemic antimicrobial administration, the dose administered via IVRLP should be subtracted from the total systemic dose to avoid systemic toxicity. When combined with systemic administration, cephalic or saphenous IVRLP in the anesthetized foal is considered an effective technique for achieving adequate systemic antimicrobial concentrations and supraphysiologic antimicrobial concentrations in the tissues and synovial compartments of the limbs. While IVRLP in foals is commonly performed in equine practice, appropriate technique is essential to maximize the clinical effect. This tutorial video is intended to provide practitioners with basic instruction for proper technique of IVRLP using the cephalic or saphenous vein in the anesthetized foal.

title: Co-contamination of aquatic food animals by microplastics, heavy metals, and pesticides: bioaccumulation, human health risk, and role of artificial intelligence.
abstract: Aquatic food animals provide essential proteins, omega-3 fatty acids, and micronutrients to billions of people worldwide, yet their safety is increasingly challenged by the co-occurrence of microplastics (MPs), heavy metals (HMs), and pesticides in aquatic ecosystems. Unlike previous reviews that examine these contaminant classes separately, this review presents an integrated framework linking contamination sources, bioaccumulation, trophic transfer, human health risks, food security, and regulatory responses. MPs can act as physicochemical vectors by adsorbing HMs and pesticides and releasing them following gastrointestinal desorption (the Trojan horse mechanism), although the importance of this pathway depends on polymer characteristics, weathering, gut conditions, and ambient contaminant concentrations. Co-exposure may produce synergistic, additive, or antagonistic effects depending on contaminant combinations, exposure conditions, and biological endpoints, highlighting that synergism should not be assumed universally. Human health risk assessment indices are evaluated alongside international regulatory guidance, with emphasis on their limitations as screening-level tools that do not account for contaminant interactions and are sensitive to exposure assumptions. The implications of co-contamination for all four FAO pillars of food security are examined through regional case studies of seafood-dependent populations. Machine learning and explainable AI applications for contaminant detection, environmental monitoring, and bioaccumulation prediction are evaluated and compared across four application domains, distinguishing proof-of-concept studies from regulatory-ready applications. Finally, key research priorities, including mixture toxicology, standardized nanoplastic analysis, long-term biomonitoring in data-sparse regions, and robust ML model validation, are identified to support future research and evidence-based seafood safety governance.

title: Left Ventricular Volume Indexing in Athletic Brazilian Sport Horses Using Body Weight.
abstract: Left ventricular (LV) volume assessment evaluates cardiac size and remodelling in horses. Single-plane Simpson method of discs (SMOD) provides volumetric measurements requiring body size normalization. We described LV volumes using SMOD in healthy Brazilian Sport Horses (BH) and evaluated thoracic-girth-estimated body weight (BWe) versus scale-measured weight (BWs) for indexing. Thirty BH horses (15 males, 15 females; 4-16 years) underwent echocardiography. LV end-diastolic (LVEDV), end-systolic volumes (LVESV), and ejection fraction (EF%) were obtained using SMOD. Body weight was scale-measured and estimated via thoracic girth formula. Volumes were indexed to BWs, BWe, and a 500-kg reference. Mean LVEDV was 1060 ± 154 mL (95% CI: 1003-1118), LVESV 318 ± 77 mL (95% CI: 290-347), and EF 70.0 ± 5.4%. Overall, BWe was associated with BWs (R² = 0.61; P < 0.0001) with mean bias of +33.25 kg (limits of agreement: -37.59 to +104.09 kg), mean absolute error of 39 ± 28.83 kg, and percentage error of 8.92 ± 7.27%. LVEDV/BWs averaged 2.30 ± 0.29 mL/kg and LVEDV/BWe 2.15 ± 0.26 mL/kg. Normalization to 500 kg yielded LVEDV[500] of 1151 ± 146 and 1069 ± 131 mL, and LVESV[500] of 346 ± 83 and 321 ± 70 mL (BWs; BWe). Indexed variables showed moderate to strong linear association between methods. In this sample, no sex or age differences were detected. Body weight normalization improved interindividual comparability. While BWe offers a practical field alternative, estimation errors warrant caution in individual evaluations, making BWs preferred.

title: Factors associated with embryo recovery in mares: A retrospective multicenter analysis and practical overview of embryo flushing protocols.
abstract: Embryo recovery (ER) is a major determinant of efficiency in equine embryo-transfer programs and may be influenced by biological, management, and technical factors. This retrospective multicenter study aimed to identify factors associated with positive ER and to describe the embryo-flushing (EF) techniques used in three commercial embryo-transfer programs. We hypothesized that factors associated with ER would differ among clinics because of differences in mare populations, semen types, management practices, and flushing systems. The study included 2861 EF cycles: 465 cycles from 196 mares in Clinic 1, 661 cycles from 265 mares in Clinic 2, and 1735 cycles from 277 mares in Clinic 3. Factors associated with positive ER were evaluated separately for each clinic using multivariable generalized linear mixed models, with mare identity included as a random intercept. Additional univariable analyses were used to examine selected factors individually. Overall ER was 55.7%, 51.4%, and 73.5% in Clinics 1, 2, and 3, respectively. In the multivariable analyses, none of the evaluated fixed effects were significantly associated with ER in Clinic 1. In Clinic 2, semen type was the only significant fixed effect, with greater odds of ER using chilled than frozen semen (OR = 2.07, 95% CI: 1.37-3.11; p < 0.001). Clinic 3 used fresh semen exclusively, and donor mare age was the only significant fixed effect, with the odds of ER decreasing by 9% for each additional year of age (OR = 0.91, 95% CI: 0.88-0.94; p < 0.001). Although the overall effect of season phase was not significant in Clinic 3, ER was lower during mid-season than early season (OR = 0.67, 95% CI: 0.46-0.99; p = 0.043). Mare identity had a significant random effect in all three clinics (p ≤ 0.05), indicating substantial between-mare variability. Repeated EF within the same season did not reduce ER in any clinic, including among mares undergoing four or more cycles. In the additional analyses, multiple ovulation was associated with higher ER in Clinics 1 and 3 but not in Clinic 2. In Clinic 2, experienced operators showed a tendency toward higher ER than less experienced operators (52.4% vs. 37.7%; p = 0.06). In conclusion, factors associated with ER differed among clinical settings. The consistent mare effect, the absence of a decline in ER with repeated flushing, and the potential influence of operator experience emphasize the importance of individual mare fertility and clinic-specific management when evaluating the efficiency of commercial embryo-transfer programs.

title: A Selective Bis-Catecholate Siderophore-Ampicillin Conjugate Expands Activity against Multidrug-Resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is a global public health crisis, with multidrug-resistant P. aeruginosa among the most critical threats. The high cost and slow pace of novel antibiotic development, coupled with rapid resistance evolution, demand innovative strategies. Here, we present a Trojan horse approach using siderophore-antibiotic conjugates (SACs) to hijack bacterial iron uptake systems and deliver β-lactam payloads across the Gram-negative outer membrane. We designed a series of ampicillin conjugates with mono-catecholate, bis-catecholate, and catecholate-hydroxamate siderophores. These conjugates demonstrate potent antimicrobial activity. Notably, the lead compound, BC-2-Amp, shows broad-spectrum and highly selective activity against a panel of 105 clinical isolates of P. aeruginosa. Mechanistic studies demonstrated that BC-2-Amp utilizes PiuA as a critical receptor for targeted delivery. Complementary in vivo experiments further confirmed its promising therapeutic efficacy. Collectively, these findings establish SACs as a potent strategy for broadening the spectrum of β-lactam antibiotics and provide a robust platform for high-potency drug delivery.

title: Fluorescent tagging for assessment of environmental cleaning in an equine hospital.
abstract: Healthcare-associated infections increase morbidity, mortality, and treatment costs in both human and veterinary medicine, and environmental contamination can contribute to their occurrence. Monitoring of environmental cleaning is an important component of multimodal infection control strategies. Fluorescent tagging is a low-cost, practical approach that correlates with reduced environmental contamination in human and small animal hospitals. Its applicability in equine hospitals, where surface characteristics and contamination risks differ, has not yet been evaluated. To evaluate fluorescent tagging as a monitoring tool for environmental cleaning in an equine hospital, to assess the impact of active feedback, and to validate an objective ImageJ-based assessment against subjective evaluation. Before-after study. A commercial fluorescent dye was applied to surfaces in examination rooms and stalls. Fluorescent tag removal was evaluated visually and objectively using standardised photography and ImageJ-based green intensity analysis. Surfaces were sampled repeatedly across two study phases, separated by structured feedback to cleaning staff. Aerobic colony counts (ACC) were performed during phase II adjacent to fluorescent tags to assess bacterial contamination before and after cleaning. Objective ImageJ-based analysis accurately distinguished between removed, partially removed, and not removed fluorescent tags, and there was strong agreement with subjective visual assessment. In examination rooms, provision of feedback resulted in a significant overall improvement in cleaning efficacy, particularly in orthopaedic treatment rooms (room1: log-odds ratio = 1.71; q-value = 0.033, room2: log-odds ratio = 2.11; q-value = 0.01), whereas no improvement was observed in stables (q-value >0.05). The ACC were not associated with fluorescent tag removal grades (q-value >0.05). Subjective and objective assessments were performed by the same non-blinded examiner, single centre design and limited ACC assessment. Fluorescent tagging is a feasible monitoring method for assessing environmental cleaning efficacy in an equine hospital, and objective quantification correlated closely with subjective visual assessment. Active feedback improved cleaning performance in examination rooms but not in stables.

title: Arthropod-Related Health Threats (ARHTs) and Nuisance Arthropods in North Khorasan Province, Iran: A Comprehensive Review.
abstract: The arthropod vectors, such as mosquitoes, sand flies, and ticks, transmit various pathogens to humans and animals, leading to public health issues. Therefore, an effective disease surveillance system is essential to provide information on these diseases in order to monitor their trends worldwide. The current study focused on the prevalence of arthropod-borne diseases and their vectors in North Khorasan Province located in northeastern Iran, bordering Turkmenistan. A narrative literature review was conducted to analyze the status of arthropod-related health threats (ARHTs) and their vectors in this area. Sources with no time limit up to 2025 were examined from PubMed, Google Scholar, ScienceDirect, and Web of Science databases using keywords like vector, arthropod, North Khorasan, and Iran. After excluding duplicates and irrelevant content, a final list of 31 papers was thoroughly evaluated. This province exhibits the occurrence of several major ARHTs, including visceral leishmaniasis, cutaneous leishmaniasis, West Nile fever, chikungunya, Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, Q fever, Theileria infection, equine piroplasmosis, dirofilariasis, Dipylidium caninum infection, fascioliasis, hymenolepiasis, scorpionism, spider bites, pediculosis, and myiasis. Given the complex and diverse ecosystem of North Khorasan, implementing tailored and innovative strategies is essential for effective surveillance and early detection of arthropod-borne diseases, thus enabling timely and efficient management of these health threats.

title: Clonal articular cartilage progenitors outperform mesenchymal stromal cells in mitigating post-traumatic osteoarthritis.
abstract: This study aimed to compare the functional, pathological, and immunomodulatory properties of articular chondroprogenitors (ACPs) with those of bone-marrow-derived mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) in preventing the progression of post-traumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA) after destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM) injury in a mouse model. ACP and MSC were isolated from three horses and assessed for their immunomodulatory capacity in vitro. Aliquots of selected ACP clones and MSCs were injected intra-articularly into male mice 1-week post destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM). The functional mobility of the mice before the injury and at weeks 2, 4, and 8 post-injury was assessed by two methods: ANY-maze™ voluntary mobility monitoring and DigiGait™ compulsory gait analysis. Upon euthanasia, joints were collected for histological scoring. In vitro assessments demonstrated that ACPs and MSCs had anti-inflammatory properties: both treatments produced lower levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, while only the ACPs produced more anti-inflammatory cytokines than controls. In vivo, both ACPs and MSCs lessened the effects of DMM on mobility. Histological scoring revealed significant reductions of PTOA in the medial compartment with ACPs relative to both MSCs and vehicle controls. Overall, ACPs effectively reduced PTOA progression to a greater extent than MSCs. Our findings demonstrated that both equine ACP and MSC treatments provided symptom modification over vehicle controls in a short-term animal study. Notably, ACPs may be more efficacious than MSCs at reducing structural joint pathology.

title: Equine (Equus caballus) primary post-natal brain-derived cells: immortalization and preliminary reprogramming attempts to induced pluripotent stem cells.
abstract: Equines represent an underexplored yet highly relevant model for studying neurological diseases within a One Health framework. Here, we report the first establishment of post-natal equine brain-derived in vitro systems, including equine primary post-natal brain-derived cells (EpBCs) and their immortalized counterparts (EiBCs). EpBCs were isolated from the hippocampus and successfully expanded, while immortalization via Simian virus 40 large T antigen generated EiBCs lines with distinct transcriptomic reprogramming characterized by cell cycle activation and partial dedifferentiation. Despite testing three non-integrating approaches-Sendai virus, episomal vectors, and synthetic mRNA-no induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs)-like colonies were detected under the tested conditions, possibly reflecting a combination of species-specific, cell-intrinsic, and donor-specific factors, as well as culture conditions, factor compatibility, and delivery efficiency. Together, these findings establish a foundational equine brain-derived cell platform and highlight key challenges in equine reprogramming. Its One Health relevance is prospective, as this system may support future comparative neurological research and the development of equine brain organoids.

title: Bioactivity profiling of linear venom peptides from Italian small wood-scorpion (Euscorpius italicus).
abstract: Rising host-expansion and the global spread of pest insects, confront agricultural sectors with substantial concerns. A promising source of potential lead compounds to target these growing challenges are animal venoms which abound with a huge diversity of bioactive peptides suited for both pest control and drug discovery. Arachnids in particular contribute substantially to the extreme diversity of highly adapted venom compounds, and for some of these, translational potential in pest control has already been demonstrated. Members of the Euscorpiidae family of scorpions are among the most successful groups of scorpions in Europe. Although they use their venom for hunting, none of their toxins has thus far been functionally evaluated as their low toxicity to humans has kept them out of the spotlight of venom research. We hypothesize that their venom peptides exert insecticidal activity which might be harnessed for pest control applications. Based on our hypothesis, we conducted bioactivity profiling of linear venom peptides derived from Euscorpius italicus, one of the most common euscorpiid species. In silico analyses revealed them as neutral to cationaic alpha helical peptides with high hydrophobicity. Functionally, our established profiling pipeline that combines in vivo and in vitro bioassays, reveals that one of the tested linear venom peptides, Ei1, causes mortality in Drosophila suzukii postinjection, as well as signs of neuroparalysis. Furthermore, Ei1 exhibits inhibitory effects on Staphylococcus aureus, while also affecting MDCK II cells and equine erythrocytes, implying functions in host defense. This study reveals insights on properties of Euscorpiidae venom, their ecological values for predation and defensive function against microbial colonization of the venom glands - revealing further knowledge to the growing biodiscovery of animal venoms and potential agricultural functions as a biological insecticide. © 2026 The Author(s). title: EUCAST disk diffusion: Can Mueller-Hinton agar with 5% sheep blood (MH-S) be an alternative medium for fastidious organisms?
journal: Clinical microbiology and infection : the official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
abstract: EUCAST recommends Mueller-Hinton (MH) agar with defibrinated horse blood and β-NAD (MH-F) for disk diffusion testing of fastidious organisms, but MH-F has been difficult to access in several geographical areas. The objective of this study was to evaluate MH with sheep blood (MH-S) as an alternative medium. Disk diffusion (DD) was performed according to EUCAST recommendations on MH-F and MH-S in parallel. All species with breakpoints on MH-F agar were tested, except for Haemophilus influenzae due to its inadequate growth on MH-S. Growth and zone diameters from parallel tests on MH-F and MH-S were compared and categorical agreement was calculated according to EUCAST recommendations. Essential agreement and bias were calculated adapting the recommendations for MIC evaluations in ISO 20776-2. Also, zone diameter distributions on MH-S produced from MH agar from three manufacturers were compared. Growth on MH-S was equally good as on MH-F for all tested species. Correlation between DD results on MH-S and MH-F was good, with 61-85, 89-100 and 95-100% inhibition zone diameters within 1, 2 and 3 mm, respectively, for each species/organism group. Systematic deviation (bias) for MH-S was below ±30% when analysed per species and for 25 of 32 agents when analysed per agent. Specific reading instructions were required for trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole vs. Streptococcus groups A, B, C and G when tested on MH-S. Inhibition zone diameters on MH-S were not significantly influenced by the three brands of MH investigated. MH-S can be used for DD for all species with EUCAST zone diameter breakpoints on MH-F (except H. influenzae, which does not grow on MH-S). Since MH-F supports growth of more species than MH-S, EUCAST will continue to recommend MH-F as the standard EUCAST medium for disk diffusion testing of fastidious organisms, unless otherwise stated. Updated information is available on the EUCAST website.

title: Experts recommend management strategies for horses during poor air quality.
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
abstract: To adapt the existing air quality index (AQI) framework to communicate equine health risk and develop practical recommendations for horse care, training, and competitions at increasing levels of air pollution. A 3-round modified Delphi study. 15 expert equine veterinarians contributed, with 11 experts completing 3 rounds. First, experts agreed that both healthy horses and those with underlying health conditions may experience short- and long-term health effects. Second, experts adapted the AQI public health messaging to communicate equine-specific health risk. Third, experts developed practical recommendations for each AQI category, spanning general management, training, and competition decisions. This study utilized the existing AQI framework to develop resources for communicating equine health risk and expert-informed management strategies for each AQI category. Reliance on translational data highlights a critical need for future work prioritizing equine-specific research on health impacts and pollutant thresholds to support refinement of AQI-based guidance. Equine veterinarians are encouraged to widely distribute this equine-specific AQI framework to clients, barn managers, and trainers as a practical framework for informed decision-making to support horse health and welfare during periods of poor air quality.

title: Wolbachia outcompetes mosquito-borne viruses by reprogramming host ATPSβ1-driven ATP metabolism toward symbiotic proliferation.
abstract: Wolbachia endosymbionts confer broad-spectrum resistance to mosquito-borne viruses. While the antiviral metabolites in Wolbachia-Aedes have been identified during viral replication, the core metabolic gene underlying this defense across the entire viral infection cycle remains undefined. Here, we demonstrated for the first time that Wolbachia strongly suppressed the emerging alphavirus Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus, extending its known antiviral spectrum. Transcriptomic and functional analyses revealed ATP synthase beta subunit 1 (ATPSβ1) as a key metabolic hub hijacked by both MBV and the symbiont. Without Wolbachia symbiosis, dengue virus and VEEV induced ATPSβ1 to promote viral binding via the viral envelope protein and increased intracellular ATP production for viral replication. Conversely, Wolbachia overrode ATPSβ1-mediated viral binding and redirected ATPSβ1-driven ATP synthesis to fuel its proliferation, strengthening antiviral activity. Pharmacologically, adenosine increased Wolbachia wAlbB density and potently suppressed viral infection in Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus cells. Oligomycin reduced intracellular ATP and inhibited viral infection in Wolbachia-free Ae. aegypti cells. Collectively, Wolbachia repurposes dual-functional ATPSβ1, which governs MBV binding and replication, into a potent antiviral effector through a metabolic tug-of-war over host ATP during symbiont-virus competition. Moreover, we highlight interventions targeting the ATPSβ1-driven metabolism as promising strategies to curb MBV transmission.

title: Serum and uterine fluid extracellular vesicles and prostaglandin E metabolite concentrations during diestrus and early pregnancy in mares.
abstract: Prostaglandins produced by endometrial and conceptus tissues have an established role in maintaining luteal function in early pregnancy and initiating luteolysis during diestrus in mares. The cellular mechanisms controlling the secretion and delivery of prostaglandins have not been fully elucidated. We hypothesized that nanosized lipid bilayer extracellular vesicles (EV) that carry a variety of biological molecules would be involved in these key regulatory processes. Serum and uterine fluid samples were collected from diestrus and pregnant mares on day (D) 10 and D14 post-ovulation, and conceptuses were collected in pregnant mare cycles and cultured for 2-3 h. Extracellular vesicles were isolated using membrane affinity spin columns. Metabolomic EV cargo was assessed using LC-MS/MS, and cytosolic phospholipase A2 (cPLA2) with immunoblotting. Serum and uterine fluid PGEM and conceptus PGE2 concentrations were compared using ELISA. Prostaglandins were below detection limits in all EV serum and uterine fluid eluates. PGEM concentrations in uterine fluid and serum did not differ between pregnant and diestrus mares at these time points. Day 10 and D14 conceptuses produced PGE2. Serum and uterine fluid EV contained AA and cPLA2. While AA abundance did not differ by reproductive status or day at these time points, uterine fluid EV AA abundance was 83 times higher than serum. Serum and uterine fluid EV carry activatable phospholipases and rate-limiting substrates for prostaglandin production rather than the prostaglandins themselves. High levels of AA in uterine fluid EV are likely important in the local regulation of uterine prostaglandin production.

title: Evaluating a novel automatic feeding device for hay provision in horses: behavioral outcomes in group and individual housing.
abstract: This study evaluated a novel Automatic Feeding Device (AFD) for hay provision in group-housed and individually housed horses. In Phase 1 (P1), behavioral responses to ground hay feeding (Control-Hay) and to hay delivery through the AFD were assessed in three group-housed mares under two conditions: AFD continuously open (O-AFD) and AFD alternating between open and closed periods (OC-AFD). In Phase 2 (P2), four individually housed horses were used to evaluate the behavioral effects of three AFD opening-closing schedules: long opening (LO-OP), medium opening (ME-OP), and short opening (SH-OP). Behavioral data were collected by continuous video recording. Data were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models, with treatment as fixed effect and horse as random effect (experimental unit). Principal component analysis was used to explore variability in agonistic behaviors among group-housed horses. In P1, individual differences in foraging activity and agonistic behaviors were observed. Exploratory behaviors increased significantly when the AFD alternated between open and closed periods compared with when it remained open (3.93 ± 3.36 vs. 1.72 ± 3.86 min/h; p = 0.010). Compared with Control-Hay, which resulted in no residual hay, AFD delivery increased residual hay, averaging 3.98 ± 0.77 kg in O-AFD and 4.88 ± 1.00 kg in OC-AFD (p < 0.001). Social hierarchy strongly influenced access to the AFD in group-housed horses. In P2, foraging from the AFD declined progressively from LO-OP and ME-OP to SH-OP (46.91 ± 0.81, 42.80 ± 1.65, and 38.84 ± 0.89 min/h, respectively; p < 0.001). Stress-related behaviors directed toward the AFD were most frequent during SH-OP: pawing occurred up to seven to eight times more often than in LO-OP and ME-OP, while rubbing and teeth or tongue use were approximately two to three times higher. Residual hay increased progressively as access duration decreased (p < 0.001), accompanied by a slight reduction in hay intake rate. Behavioral responses to the AFD were influenced by social dynamics in group-housed horses and feeder access schedule in individually-housed horses. The medium opening interval (40 min open, 20 min closed) appeared to provide the most appropriate balance between regulating hay intake, maintaining feeding behavior and limiting stress-related behaviors.

title: Retrospective serological evidence of exposure to selected equine viruses in horses from Indigenous communities of Costa Rica, 2011.
abstract: Horses are essential for transportation and livelihoods in Indigenous communities of Costa Rica. However, information on their exposure to viral pathogens remains scarce. We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional serosurvey using samples collected from horses from four Indigenous communities (Alto Pacuare, Amubre, Paso Marcos, and Vereh) sampled between March and October 2011 (n = 278). Sera were tested in 2014 using commercial immunodiffusion or ELISA assays for antibodies against West Nile virus (WNV), equine herpesviruses 1 and 4 (EHV-1 and EHV-4), influenza A virus, equine arteritis virus (EAV), and equine infectious anemia virus (EIAV). Seroprevalence estimates and Wilson 95% confidence intervals were calculated, and differences among communities were assessed using Pearson's chi-square or Fisher's exact tests, as appropriate. The number of tested sera differed across assays due to sample availability. Serological evidence compatible with WNV exposure was detected in 58.9% (139/236) of horses, with the highest proportion in Amubre (83.3%). EHV-4 showed consistently high seropositivity (91.2%, 125/137), whereas EHV-1 seroprevalence was low (6.6%, 9/137). Antibodies to influenza A virus and EAV were detected at low frequencies (5.1%, 12/237, and 3.0%, 7/236, respectively). EIAV seroprevalence reached 16.6% (35/211), with the highest proportion in Paso Marcos (23.8%). Significant differences among communities were observed for WNV, influenza A virus, and EHV-4 seropositivity. These findings represent historical serological evidence of exposure in 2011 and should not be interpreted as reflecting current viral circulation. Nevertheless, they provide a retrospective baseline for comparison with future surveillance and highlight the value of including underserved Indigenous equine populations in disease-monitoring and prevention programs.

title: Coronoidectomy for treatment of osteomyelitis of the coronoid process: A novel technique.
abstract: To report a minimally invasive coronoidectomy technique for the treatment of osteomyelitis of the mandibular coronoid process. 2-year-old Haflinger mare. Case report. A 2-year-old Haflinger mare presented with a 6-week history of a non-healing wound caudodorsal to the left eye over the supraorbital fossa. A moderate amount of purulent, hemorrhagic discharge was present with a mild degree of soft tissue swelling. The horse was reactive to palpation of the region. Radiographic examination did not reveal any osseous abnormalities or foreign material in the wound tract. Computed tomography findings were consistent with chronic osteomyelitis of the left coronoid process of the mandible. A minimally invasive coronoidectomy was performed under general anesthesia to remove the left coronoid process of the mandible. The coronoid process of the mandible was successfully removed and the wound healed. No complications were reported postoperatively. At 1 year postoperatively the horse was being used for its intended purpose, and the owner deemed the outcome successful. The surgical technique reported presents a minimally invasive approach to excise the mandibular coronoid process in a single case.

title: Feasibility of Enucleation in Standing Sedated Horses With Retrobulbar Anesthesia and Auriculopalpebral Nerve Block: Impact of Ultrasound Guidance in a Case Series.
abstract: Examining the feasibility of enucleation in standing sedated horses with dorsal retrobulbar anesthesia (RBA) and auriculopalpebral (AP) nerve block and the impact of ultrasound (US) guidance on RBA success. Thirty horses. In a prospective clinical case series, horses (n = 15/group) received standardized sedation, dorsal RBA (12 mL mepivacaine) and AP nerve block (4 mL lidocaine). Group 1 received US-assisted RBA (10 MHz linear probe), Group 2 underwent blind RBA subsequently. Needle positioning time was recorded. Eyelid sensitivity was measured before (t0) and 20 min after injection (t20). RBA success was defined as surgical tolerance at t20. US image quality (excellent/good/poor) was assessed and compared with RBA success. If RBA failed, additional local anesthetic was injected. RBA success was 63.4% (19/30) with 73.3% (11/15) in Group 1 and 53.3% (8/15) in Group 2 (p = 0.179). 3/19 successful cases required additional retrobulbar anesthetic top ups intraoperatively (t60-t80). A significant association was found between the number of successfully anesthetized lid areas per horse and RBA success (p < 0.001). Mean time for US-assisted RBA was 5.2 min (±1.7 min). US image quality was rated as "excellent" in 3/15, "good" in 7/15, and "poor" in 5/15 cases, with corresponding success rates of 100% (3/3), 85.7% (6/7), and 40% (2/5), respectively. Improved US image quality showed a non-significant trend toward higher success (p = 0.053). RBA combined with AP nerve block provides adequate anesthesia for standing equine enucleation. US image quality and eyelid sensitivity are suitable block success predictors.

title: Comparative effects of copper oxide nanoparticle morphology (nanorods vs. nanospheres) on the metabolism and swimming performance of Oreochromis niloticus.
abstract: The increasing production of nanomaterials has raised concerns regarding their environmental presence and potential adverse effects on non-target aquatic species. This study investigated the physiological impacts of acute (24 h) exposure of Oreochromis niloticus to copper oxide nanoparticles (CuO-NPs) of two distinct morphologies: nanorods (NRs) and nanospheres (NSs). Nanoparticles were synthesized and characterized via transmission electron microscopy, revealing significant differences in size, shape, and colloidal stability. Juvenile tilapia was exposed to concentrations ranging from 50 to 800 µg/L to evaluate routine metabolism (specific oxygen consumption), ammonia excretion, and swimming performance to fatigue. Both NRs and NSs significantly altered physiological parameters with distinct patterns. Oxygen consumption increased dose-dependently, reaching a 51% elevation with NRs (400 µg/L) and up to 254% with NSs (800 µg/L). Ammonia excretion was significantly inhibited in groups exposed to NRs. At 200 µg/L, excretion was nearly three times lower than in the control group, suggesting disturbances in gill function. In contrast, NSs induced significant increases in ammonia excretion (up to 127% at 800 µg/L), likely associated with enhanced protein catabolism. Swimming performance was also severely impaired, with NRs causing up to a 55% reduction in time to fatigue (200 µg/L), indicating locomotor and neuromuscular compromise. Comparative analysis showed that nanorods were consistently more toxic, supporting the "Trojan horse" hypothesis, likely due to their higher aggregation tendency and consequent release of CU2+ ions. These findings underscore the critical role of morphology, colloidal stability, and solubility in the ecotoxicological assessment of nanomaterials. We conclude that CuO-NPs, particularly in the form of nanorods, pose a significant risk to fish physiology and locomotor performance, reinforcing the need to integrate morphological, physiological, and behavioral endpoints in environmental risk assessment and regulatory policies for the safe use of these nanomaterials.

title: Platelet-Based Blood Products in Bovine and Equine Medicine: A Systematic Scoping Review of Blood Collection, Preparation Methods, and Reporting Completeness.
abstract: Platelet-based blood products, including platelet-rich plasma, platelet concentrate, and platelet lysate, are increasingly investigated in veterinary medicine as biological preparations with proposed regenerative, anti-inflammatory, and immunomodulatory properties. In bovine and equine medicine, their use has expanded across several clinical fields, but blood collection and product preparation methods have not been systematically synthesized. This systematic scoping review aimed to describe the literature on platelet-based blood products in bovine and equine medicine, summarize methodological characteristics of blood collection and preparation methods, and analyze studies addressing bovine mammary disorders. Searches were performed in Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, CAB Abstracts, and PubMed on 25 August 2026, with no publication-year or start-date restriction. Eligible studies were original peer-reviewed articles in English; fibrin- or gel-based preparations were excluded when the corresponding liquid platelet-based product could not be separately characterized or evaluated, as were scaffold or combined constructs when the platelet-based component could not be evaluated separately. No formal review protocol was registered or published. Studies providing eligible bovine and/or equine data and reporting at least one methodological aspect related to collection, preparation, activation or lysis, storage, characterization, or administration were eligible. A total of 191 studies were included. Studies contributing equine data only among the target species predominated (161/191; 84.3%), whereas 29 studies (15.2%) contributed bovine data only and one study (0.5%) included both bovine and equine data. The PRP family, including PRP and related PRP-type preparations, was the most frequently investigated product group (134/191; 70.2%), followed by platelet lysate (46/191; 24.1%) and platelet concentrate (19/191; 9.9%); categories were not mutually exclusive. Methods varied in donor source, collection site, blood volume, anticoagulant, collection system, centrifugation workflow, activation or lysis, storage, and characterization. The main blood collection and preparation workflow was reconstructable in 111 studies (58.1%) and partially reconstructable in 80 studies (41.9%). Methodological reporting was frequently incomplete, particularly for leukocyte concentration, activation or lysis procedures, storage conditions, and product-level sterility or microbiological quality control. Product-level sterility or microbiological quality control was explicitly reported in 7 studies (3.7%) and partially reported in one study (0.5%). Only five studies addressed bovine mammary disorders and investigated methodologically distinct products. More complete and consistent methodological reporting is needed to improve reproducibility and comparability across studies.

title: Occurrence of Clostridium perfringens and Molecular Detection of Clostridioides difficile Toxin-Gene Targets in Foal Fecal Samples: A Multiregional Study in Türkiye.
abstract: Clostridium perfringens and Clostridioides difficile are associated with equine enterocolitis, but data on foals in Türkiye are limited. This multiregional study examined 300 archived fecal samples from 2-6-month-old foals originating from 20 stud farms in five provinces. Gastrointestinal signs were recorded in ten foals; systematic clinical information was unavailable for 290. Clostridium perfringens was investigated by anaerobic culture followed by PCR confirmation and toxin-gene profiling (cpa, cpb, cpb2, etx, iap, cpe, and netB). Clostridioides difficile-specific DNA was investigated by PCR of DNA extracted from archived fecal material, targeting tpi, tcdA, and tcdB. Clostridium perfringens was confirmed in 50/300 samples (16.7%; 95% CI, 12.9-21.3%); confirmed isolates had a cpa-only profile among the genes investigated. The tpi target was detected in 12/300 samples (4.0%; 95% CI, 2.3-6.9%), of which seven also contained tcdA and tcdB (2.3% overall; 95% CI, 1.1-4.7%). cpa-confirmed C. perfringens and the C. difficile-specific tpi target was detected in samples from all five provinces; geographic comparisons were descriptive and exploratory. Because C. difficile was not cultured and toxin production was not assessed, the results represent species-specific and toxin-gene targets rather than viable toxigenic isolates or active disease. Clinical associations could not be evaluated. These findings provide multiregional baseline data and support prospective studies incorporating clinical assessment, culture, quantitative testing, and toxin detection.

title: Retrospective Serological Survey of Equine Influenza Virus and Piroplasm Parasites in Free-Ranging Wild Equids from Kenya and Tanzania.
abstract: Wild equids may act as reservoirs for infectious pathogens affecting domestic equine populations, yet data on exposure to equine infectious anemia virus (EIAV), equine influenza virus (EIV), and equine piroplasmosis agents in African wildlife remain scarce. Our objectives were to retrospectively determine serological evidence of exposure to EIAV, EIV, Theileria equi, and Babesia caballi among Grevy's zebras and rhinoceroses from Kenya and Tanzania. A total of 284 archived serum samples from 215 Grevy's zebras and 69 rhinoceroses were analyzed using commercial ELISAs. Positive EIAV screening tests were retested using a second confirmatory assay. No confirmed EIAV antibodies were detected in zebras or rhinoceroses. Antibodies against EIV were identified in 20/215 zebras (9.3%), all originating from Serengeti National Park. Theileria equi antibodies were detected in 194/206 zebras (94.2%), while Babesia caballi antibodies were detected in 8/206 zebras (3.9%). Rhinoceroses were negative for all pathogens tested. This study provides evidence of widespread exposure of Grevy's zebras to T. equi and limited exposure to EIV in East Africa while failing to identify serologic evidence of EIAV infection in zebras or rhinoceroses. These findings improve understanding of infectious disease ecology at the wildlife-livestock interface and support continued wildlife surveillance programs.

title: Antiviral Activity of Naringenin Against Equine Alphaherpesvirus Type 8 In Vitro.
abstract: Equine alphaherpesvirus type 8 (EHV-8) is an economically significant emerging pathogen responsible for severe respiratory disease, reproductive failure, and neurological disorders in equids worldwide. The escalating prevalence of EHV-8 in large-scale donkey farming operations, particularly in China, has resulted in substantial economic losses; however, no licensed antiviral agents or prophylactic vaccines are currently available. In the present study, we evaluated the anti-EHV-8 activity of naringenin in susceptible cells and comprehensively explored the underlying molecular mechanisms. Our results demonstrated that naringenin markedly inhibited EHV-8 infection in RK-13 and NBL-6 cells in a dose-dependent manner. Moreover, naringenin blocked the replication of EHV-8 via HO-1 (heme oxygenase-1)-mediated type I interferon (IFN) response. Collectively, our findings indicate that naringenin may serve as a promising therapeutic drug for the treatment of EHV-8 infection.

title: Detection of Shamonda Virus in Two Horses with Neurological Signs in Germany.
abstract: Shamonda virus (SHAV), which has recently emerged in Central Europe and has caused disease in numerous cattle herds, was detected in brain tissue from two horses that showed clinical signs, including neurological disorder, and underwent pathological examination. The horses reportedly exhibited seizure-like episodes (Horse A) as well as fever and ataxia (Horse B). In both horses, severe lymphohistiocytic meningoencephalitis with hemorrhages was observed in various parts of the central nervous system (CNS), while outside the CNS no abnormalities were found. The virus genome could be detected by RT-qPCR in all examined parts of the CNS of both horses. In a postmortem cerebrospinal fluid sample of one horse, the virus could only be detected with a very low genome load; however, postmortem contamination cannot be completely ruled out. Consistent with the histological findings, no SHAV genome was detected in either the blood or organs outside the CNS. Postmortem, CNS material-especially brainstem tissue-is suitable for detection of histological lesions and virus genomes via RT-qPCR, while intravital diagnostics of a SHAV infection in horses exhibiting neurological signs is at the moment only possible to a very limited extent. The epidemiological role of horses in the SHAV outbreak is currently unclear.

title: Generalized Tetanus in a Four-Month-Old Labrador Retriever: Complete Recovery and One-Year Follow-Up in a Rare Canine Case.
abstract: Tetanus is an infrequent, potentially fatal neurological disease in dogs, caused by tetanospasmin, the neurotoxin of Clostridium tetani, which reaches the central nervous system by retrograde axonal transport and blocks the release of the inhibitory neurotransmitters glycine and γ-aminobutyric acid. Dogs are comparatively resistant to the toxin, and canine reports remain scarce. This report describes generalized tetanus in a four-month-old, 13 kg male Labrador Retriever presented with an axillary wound sustained approximately one month earlier and neurological signs progressing over approximately seven days, from gait disturbance to generalized whole-body rigidity. On examination the dog showed trismus, risus sardonicus, cervical hyperextension, opisthotonos, third-eyelid protrusion, a sawhorse stance, hyperthermia and intermittent respiratory distress. The diagnosis was established clinically, following a structured neurological work-up and exclusion of the principal differentials, as confirmatory assays were unavailable. Total serum calcium was within the reference interval; serum creatine kinase was elevated; and venous blood-gas analysis indicated a mild, compensated metabolic acidosis. Management comprised metronidazole and clindamycin, equine tetanus antitoxin, diazepam, meloxicam and intensive nursing care in a low-stimulation environment. The dog improved from the first day of hospitalization and recovered without residual deficits, with no recurrence over one year of follow-up. The favorable outcome, in a young canine patient for which the literature would predict a guarded prognosis, is consistent with the absence of clinically detectable autonomic and cardiorespiratory dysfunction and with meticulous supportive care.

title: Native Entomophages in the Regulation Cameraria ohridella Deschka & Dimic Populations: Potential and Limitations for Control.
abstract: Cameraria ohridella Deschka & Dimić was recorded from Macedonia in the 1980s (Deschka G, Dimić N (1986)). The primary host plant is Aesculus hippocastanum. In Russia, this pest was first discovered in 2003 in Kaliningrad. Since the first introduction of C. ohridella into Europe, many studies have been conducted on C. ohridella parasitoids to identify natural control factors. In this review, we examine the spread of invasive insects identified in recent years, particularly Ohrid horse chestnut leaf miner (Cameraria ohridella Deschka & Dimić), and consider the strategies used by native parasitoids to defeat this phytophage. The review also discusses entomophages that feed on C. ohridella. Studies show that in Europe, C. ohridella is attacked by a diverse range of parasitoids-predominantly native polyphagous Hymenoptera, with the family Eulophidae predominating. The most significant species are M. frontalis, P. saulius, C. trifasciatus, and P. agraules. Significant regional differences in recorded parasitism levels-ranging from 1% to 33.6%-have been identified; these may be attributed not only to biological and ecological factors (such as host developmental stage preferences, as well as spatial, climatic, and phenological conditions) but also to the calculation methodology. The low effectiveness of the C. ohridella parasitoid complex in Europe is largely due to poor developmental synchrony between the parasitoids and their hosts. The composition of the assemblage in urban plantings is also influenced by habitat type and anthropogenic disturbance, particularly the removal of fallen leaves. Finally, we provide an overview of future research prospects, with an emphasis on the influence of parasitoids on C. ohridella population densities.

title: Association Between Gut Microbiota Dysbiosis and Synovial Inflammation in Carpal Osteoarthritis of Ili Racehorses: A Preliminary Study Integrating Imaging, Synovial Fluid Analysis, and Fecal 16S rRNA Sequencing.
journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a leading cause of lameness and premature retirement in racehorses. Gut microbiota may contribute to OA pathogenesis through the gut-joint axis, but this relationship remains unclear in racehorses. This study focused on six OA-affected Ili racehorses and six healthy Ili racehorses from the same region; the Ili horse originated from Yili, Xinjiang, China. OA severity was assessed by clinical examination, lameness grading, radiography, arthroscopy, synovial fluid biomarker analysis, and fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Associations between differential gut microbiota and synovial inflammatory markers were evaluated by Spearman correlation analysis. OA horses exhibited higher lameness scores and typical radiographic findings. Compared with healthy controls, OA horses exhibited significantly higher synovial concentrations of IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, total protein, COMP, and MMP-3. Gut microbiota analysis revealed reduced microbial diversity and significant compositional alterations in OA horses. Spearman correlation analysis demonstrated significant associations between these microbial changes and synovial inflammatory mediators as well as cartilage degradation markers. Overall, gut microbiota dysbiosis in Ili racehorses with carpal OA may be associated with synovial inflammation and abnormal cartilage metabolism via the gut-joint axis. However, the experimental scale and the number of animals will be increased as needed for further validation.

title: Cardiovascular Responses and Energy Expenditure During a Standardized Training Programme in Three-Year-Old Czech Warmblood Stallions.
journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
abstract: Early training represents an important period in the development of young sport horses, yet field-based information on cardiovascular responses and estimated energy expenditure across different exercise modalities remains limited. This study aimed to characterize heart rate (HR) responses and estimate energy expenditure in three-year-old Czech Warmblood stallions during an 18-week standardized training programme, with emphasis on exercise modality and temporal variation. We hypothesized that HR responses and estimated energy expenditure would differ among exercise modalities and vary throughout the training period. Fourteen three-year-old Czech Warmblood stallions were monitored over 18 weeks, comprising 1003 training sessions across six exercise modalities. Session mean, peak, and minimum HR were recorded, and energy expenditure was estimated using HR-based equations and National Research Council (NRC) recommendations. Linear mixed-effects models assessed associations with exercise modality and monitoring week, accounting for repeated observations within horses. Exercise modality was associated with mean HR (χ2 = 284.64, p < 0.001) and peak HR (χ2 = 122.08, p < 0.001), but not minimum HR (p = 0.066). Monitoring week was associated with all three HR outcomes (p < 0.001), with significant modality × week interactions. Estimated energy expenditure per session differed among exercise modalities (p < 0.001), with the highest model-based values observed during free jumping and horse walker exercise and the lowest during lunging. NRC-based estimates of daily energy expenditure (113.87 ± 11.73 MJ/day) exceeded estimates obtained using the Coenen HR (100.33 ± 6.23 MJ/day) and Coenen O2 (95.78 ± 6.68 MJ/day) methods. Cardiovascular responses and estimated energy expenditure differed among exercise modalities, while temporal HR variation could not be attributed solely to cardiovascular adaptation. Assessment of training load should consider both exercise characteristics and session duration. HR monitoring provides complementary information under field conditions, but HR-derived energy estimates should not be regarded as independently validated measures of energy requirements.

title: From Trauma to Innovation: A Comparative History of Limb Amputation and Prosthetics in Humans and Ungulates from Historical and Zooarchaeological Perspectives.
journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
abstract: Amputation and prosthetics represent vital themes in the history of medicine and zooarchaeology, reflecting the boundaries of therapeutic capabilities and evolving human-animal relationships. This study provides a comprehensive, comparative historical analysis of limb amputation procedures, surgical tools, haemostasis, and prosthetic rehabilitation in both humans and ungulates. A narrative literature review was conducted across electronic databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, Google Scholar, and the Cochrane Library) and digital repositories to evaluate archaeological evidence, ancient legal frameworks, and medieval/early modern medical and veterinary treatises. The historical evolution reveals striking cross-disciplinary technical analogies. Early modern surgical instruments (amputation knives and saws) and basic haemostatic approaches (fire cauterization transitioning to vascular ligation) developed along parallel trajectories in human and veterinary surgeries. However, the post-operative application of prosthetics reveals sharp biomechanical contrasts. While human prosthetics primarily addressed locomotion and cosmetics, veterinary prosthetics in heavy ungulates (horses and cattle) faced critical biological barriers, most notably contralateral limb overload leading to laminitis. Conversely, modern cases in lighter species (donkeys, alpacas, and sheep) demonstrate significantly higher adaptive success. Integrating human medical milestones with veterinary history provides a holistic framework for understanding paleopathologies and the cultural shift from culling injured livestock toward advanced, empathetic veterinary bioengineering.

title: Refining the Protocol for Equine Umbilical-Cord-Derived Mesenchymal Stem Cell Isolation: A Pilot Study on Resource Efficiency and Cellular Properties.
journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
abstract: Equine mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) are vital tools for preclinical studies and regenerative medicine, due to their multipotent nature and immunomodulatory potential. Wharton's jelly provides a non-invasive and abundant source of MSCs. However, the isolation from equine umbilical cord remains challenging, as tissue decontamination is difficult and the enzymatic isolation methods often yield variable amounts of cells. In addition, the established protocols are frequently labour-intensive, time-consuming, and costly. In this pilot study we adapted existing protocols with the aim to improve contamination rates, time commitment and costs. A thorough decontamination method and increased collagenase I digestion time from 3 h in the reference method (RM) to 24 h for the novel method (NM) were employed. Trilineage differentiation, RT-qPCR and flow cytometry were used to characterise both groups. Finally, a non-inferiority analysis was performed to confirm the feasibility of the NM. The changes in protocol led to the decrease in overtime and nightshifts, a faster postisolation expansion by reducing the culture duration by 13.5 ± 11 d, and minimised overall contamination rates (6.3% across 64 samples; RM = 3.1%, NM = 9.4%) compared with most published protocols. Consequently, we were able to reduce the costs per sample by 21 ± 21%.

title: From Microbiome Associations to Deployable Precision Probiotics in Animals: A Critical Narrative Review and Proposed Causal Evidence Framework for Next-Generation Probiotic Development.
journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
abstract: Next-generation probiotics (NGPs) are promoted as precision tools for animal health, yet the term is often applied to uncommon taxa before causality, safety and target-species efficacy are established. This critical narrative review reframes animal NGPs as a development pathway rather than a taxonomic category. A structured PubMed search was last run on 14 September 2026 with a publication date cutoff of 1 September 2026 and was supplemented by citation tracing and targeted searches of authoritative sources. From the screened literature, 45 representative and conceptually informative sources were purposively selected for the final narrative synthesis; the review was not intended to provide systematic or exhaustive coverage. The detailed synthesis focused on terrestrial farm and companion animals, whereas equine, rabbit and aquaculture studies were treated as boundary evidence. We evaluate how strain-resolved metagenomics, culturomics, metatranscriptomics, metaproteomics, metabolomics, host transcriptomics, machine learning, metabolic modeling and perturbation systems can move discovery beyond association. Studies across animal sectors show many biomarkers but limited causal validation, strain tracking, formulation data, multisite trials and ecological safety assessment. We propose an author-developed conceptual framework comprising a cumulative evidence ladder, from reproducible associations to field-ready deployment, and the ANIMAL-NGP reporting checklist (Animal endotype, Native ecological fit, Identity and genomic safety, Mechanism, Administration and manufacturing, and Longitudinal validation). These tools are intended to align claims with evidence and require prospective application and external validation. Multi-omics should therefore function as an evidence-navigation system, not as a substitute for causality.

title: Ovulation Timing After Recombinant Human Chorionic Gonadotropin, Gonadorelin, or Buserelin Under Estrus-Triggered and Fixed-Time Treatment Protocols for Artificial Insemination in Sows.
journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
abstract: Precise coordination between ovulation and insemination is essential for optimizing fixed-time artificial insemination (FTAI) in sows. This study compared ovulation timing and reproductive outcomes after treatment with recombinant human chorionic gonadotropin (rhCG), gonadorelin, or buserelin under estrus-triggered and fixed-time treatment protocols. A total of 285 sows received equine chorionic gonadotropin 24 h after weaning. In Trial 1, the ovulation-inducing treatments were administered at estrus onset, whereas in Trial 2 they were administered 72 h after equine chorionic gonadotropin. Ovulation was monitored by transabdominal ultrasonography. In Trial 1, no significant differences in ovulation timing or reproductive performance were detected among treatments. In Trial 2, no significant differences were detected among treatments in the proportion of sows with ovulation detected within 72 h (p = 0.847), the overall time-to-event distributions (log-rank p = 0.790), or the variability in detected ovulation timing (Brown-Forsythe p = 0.884). Among rhCG-treated sows in which ovulation was detected, all observed ovulations occurred between 37 and 54 h after treatment. No statistically significant differences in reproductive outcomes were detected among treatments. These findings provide new information on the temporal ovulatory response to rhCG under fixed-time treatment and may inform further refinement of insemination timing in sow FTAI protocols.

title: Apparent Ca Test Positivity and Crossmatch Reactivity in Donkeys from Italy: Intraspecies and Horse-Donkey Compatibility.
journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
abstract: Blood group distribution and serological compatibility are poorly characterized in donkeys. We estimated the apparent Ca positive-test frequency in 84 domestic donkeys and assessed donkey-donkey and horse-donkey crossmatch reactivity. Ca typing was performed using a commercial equine immunochromatographic assay. For donkey-donkey crossmatching, one major and one minor crossmatch were analyzed for each of the 77 Ca-concordant and 34 Ca-discordant pairs. Fifty-six of eighty-four donkeys yielded a positive result with the equine Ca assay (66.7%; 95% CI, 56.1-75.8%). Major combined macroscopic/microscopic reactivity occurred in 18/77 Ca-concordant and 11/34 Ca-discordant pairs, whereas minor combined reactivity occurred in 21/77 and 8/34 pairs, respectively. In crossed random-effects logistic models, the adjusted odds ratios for Ca-discordant versus Ca-concordant pairs were 1.56 (95% CI, 0.64-3.82) for major combined reactivity, 0.82 (95% CI, 0.32-2.10) for minor combined reactivity, and 1.57 (95% CI, 0.41-5.94) for major macroscopic reactivity; the minor macroscopic model was not estimable. Horse-donkey reactions were frequent and direction-dependent. When donkey plasma was tested against horse RBCs, combined reactivity occurred in 80/80 tests in the horse-donor/donkey-recipient dataset and in 76/76 tests in the reciprocal dataset, with macroscopic reactivity in 77/80 (96.3%) and 74/76 (97.4%), respectively. In the reciprocal horse-plasma/donkey-RBC direction, combined reactivity occurred in 53/80 (66.3%) and 51/76 (67.1%) tests, with macroscopic reactivity in 32/80 (40.0%) and 32/76 (42.1%), respectively. Ca concordance was not significantly associated with crossmatch reactivity in the present dataset, and Ca status alone did not account for the observed crossmatch-reactivity pattern.

title: Cranial Shape Variation in Adult Kyrgyz Horses: Associations with Size and Sex.
journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
abstract: Cranial diversity within indigenous horse populations remains incompletely characterized. Cranial shape variation and its associations with skull size and sex were investigated in 37 adult Kyrgyz horses aged 4-5 years (18 females and 19 males). Three-dimensional configurations of 25 cranial landmarks were evaluated using Procrustes alignment, principal component analysis, and permutation-based multivariate models. Skull size was quantified using centroid size calculated from the landmark configurations. The first two principal components represented 29.41% of shape variance, with changes distributed across multiple cranial regions and substantial overlap between sexes. A 5.42% greater mean centroid size was observed in males (p 0.05). Small, localized differences were observed between adjusted mean configurations. Cranial variation was therefore characterized by changes across several anatomical regions, a modest association with size, and limited evidence for additional sexual shape differentiation after size adjustment.

title: Teaching Direction Control in Horse Riding: A Pre-Post Intervention Proof-of-Concept Study Using Multi-Modal Motor Learning Techniques.
journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
abstract: Many riders experience persistent communication problems with their horses, particularly in controlling speed and direction, despite extensive training. This proof-of-concept study employed a pre-test-post-test intervention design to examine the effectiveness of the Four-Step Riding Programme (FSRP) in developing clear rider-horse body language for direction control. Multi-modal motor learning techniques (MMLTs) were applied to five rider-horse dyads during four one-hour lessons to teach coordinated movement patterns necessary for directional accuracy. Rider-horse communication was evaluated before and after the intervention using video recordings of 13 riding exercises. Three independent assessors rated the performances on a 5-point Likert scale, and riders provided self-assessments on the same scale. Horse stride parameters, reflecting shoulder control, were visualised with the Alogo™ Move Pro electronic sensor. Significant improvements were observed between pre- and post-intervention scores across all assessors and participants (p < 0.05). These preliminary findings suggest that the FSRP holds promise for facilitating the acquisition of rider-horse body language necessary for precise direction control.

title: The Western Ecotype of the Kazakh Horse: Current Status and Genomic Characterisation.
abstract: Background/Objectives: The Kazakh horse comprises several locally adapted types and ecotypes of the Eurasian Steppe. The Adai is its western ecotype, kept year-round on desert pasture in Mangystau, Western Kazakhstan, and recognised as a separate breed in 2024 without genetic evaluation. We asked whether that label corresponds to a genetic unit and whether the population has remained closed. Methods: We genotyped 533 horses recorded as Adai, 500 traced to five farms in Mangystau, against 988 reference horses of 45 breeds on 36,193 shared autosomal SNPs. Structure was assessed by principal component analysis, pairwise FST with block-jackknife intervals, neighbour-joining trees and cross-validated individual assignment; introgression per animal by an f4 statistic against an empirical null of 223 reference-steppe horses, with the ancestry scale calibrated on 1800 simulated crosses built from real genotypes; and eight body measurements were modelled within farms. Results: The Adai was not separable from the Central Asian steppe complex as a population: pairwise FST was 0.004-0.008 against Tuva, Yili, Sanhe and Mongolian horses, and two Adai farms differed from each other as much as an Adai farm differed from a reference-steppe breed. Individual assignment was nonetheless accurate against those breeds (86-100% pairwise), but the same classifier separated two herds of Adai at 69-85%, so assignment accuracy on thousands of markers tracks marker number rather than breed identity. Against the empirical null, 15.6% of Adai exceeded the 95th percentile and twelve exceeded the maximum. The estimator carries a floor of 3.7 percentage points on an unadmixed Adai; on the calibrated scale, 9.6% of animals reached the ancestry expected from one Thoroughbred great-grandparent and 4.2% that expected from one grandparent (15.8% and 4.6% uncalibrated). Introgression was concentrated: one farm carried 42% of its horses at a great-grandparent equivalent or more against 0-9% at the other four, a difference that survived every analysis accounting for family structure. Ancestry showed no within-farm association with any of eight body measurements, with or without age in the model. Conclusions: The Adai is not a differentiated population but part of a continuous steppe complex, and carries undocumented ancestry of Thoroughbred affinity concentrated in particular holdings. As managed, it cannot be certified from a document or a phenotype. Genomic verification at registration is a plausible instrument, but the marker panel it would require was not developed or validated here.

title: Epidemiology of animal bites and post-exposure vaccination coverage in Davao City, Philippines: A five-year retrospective cohort study, 2019-2023.
abstract: Rabies remains a major public health threat in the Philippines, particularly in urban areas such as Davao City, where frequent animal bites from domestic reservoirs increase the transmission risk at the human-animal-environment interface. Detailed epidemiological data on animal bites and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) coverage are limited. This One Health-framed retrospective cohort study describes trends in bite incidents, assesses PEP coverage, and identifies gaps in rabies prevention efforts from 2019 to 2023. Surveillance data from the Davao City Animal Bite Treatment Centers captured 98,442 cases. Dogs caused 63.5% of bites, with a significant upward trend (p = 0.027; τ = 1.0, 95% CI 0.200-1.800); cat bites (36.4%) rose sharply, indicating an emerging reservoir challenge. Children ≤15 years of age showed a significant increase (p = 0.027). The 3rd congressional district had the most pronounced rise across demographics and exposure categories. Tissue culture vaccine coverage remained at 100%, equine rabies immunoglobulin rose from 18.5% to 85.9%, whereas human rabies immunoglobulin remained low post-COVID. Despite universal TCV access, immunoglobulin gaps limit its control. Rising cat bites and severe exposures demand integrated One Health strategies, enhanced surveillance, animal vaccination, and supply chain strengthening, to achieve zero human rabies deaths by 2030.

title: Catastrophic distal sesamoidean ligament rupture in 72 racehorses in California.
journal: Journal of veterinary diagnostic investigation : official publication of the American Association of Veterinary Laboratory Diagnosticians, Inc
abstract: Rupture of major distal sesamoidean ligaments (DSLs) in racehorses results in suspensory apparatus failure. Our objective was to describe postmortem findings and exercise histories for Thoroughbred (TB) and Quarter Horse racehorses that had DSL rupture as the sole cause of catastrophic musculoskeletal and suspensory apparatus failure. We described horse signalment, activity at the time of injury, and postmortem findings and compared the exercise histories with those of event-matched control horses. In 72 racehorses, predominantly ≥4-y-old, catastrophic rupture of forelimb DSLs (41 left, 29 right, 2 bilateral) occurred while racing (61), training (9), or during non-exercise activity (2). DSL rupture occurred in isolation in 27 horses; the remaining 45 horses also had disruption of other ligaments and tendons secondary to associated fetlock or pastern disarticulation. Rupture of the DSLs involved the straight (69), oblique (68 medial, 69 lateral), cruciate (49), and short (49) DSLs. Complete rupture of the straight, oblique, cruciate, and short DSLs occurred more frequently (p < 0.05) in the proximal third of the pastern region (49 horses) than complete rupture of the straight and oblique DSLs in the distal third of the pastern region (23 horses). Two horses had chronic desmopathy in the proximal third of the oblique DSL. Proximal ruptures occurred more frequently in the left forelimb (p = 0.005). TB horses with DSL rupture had longer careers, more time in layup, and less high-speed activity in the year before injury than unaffected control horses. Complete rupture of the DSLs had a very low prevalence (1.4%) among catastrophic musculoskeletal injuries.

title: Thirteen years of environmental surveillance of ESKAPE organisms and Escherichia coli in an equine hospital: Informing infection control.
abstract: Bacteria from the ESKAPE group (i.e., Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Enterobacter species) and Escherichia coli are frequently multidrug-resistant and can be associated with healthcare-associated infections, an increasing concern for veterinary settings. To determine the environmental prevalence of ESKAPE and E. coli on surfaces which can act as reservoirs of infection in clinical areas in equine hospitals. Observational study. Routine environmental sampling was performed in one busy equine hospital with Swiffer® wipes to screen surfaces from high-risk areas (e.g., surgical theatres, intensive care unit [ICU], isolation unit), equipment (e.g., endotracheal tubes) and high-touch areas (e.g., keyboards) following selective species-specific protocols for each target organism. Monitoring hand-hygiene of hospital staff and students was by hand-plate sampling. After a pilot phase E. faecium was excluded from routine screening. Nine hundred and ninety-five environmental and hand-plate samples were collected from April 2010 to February 2023. The overall E. coli-SKAPE (E. coli, methicillin-resistant S. aureus [MRSA], K. pneumoniae, A. baumannii, P. aeruginosa and Enterobacter spp.) prevalence was 37.9%, where E. coli was the most (and K. pneumoniae the least) common target organism identified (18.0% and 1.7% respectively). E. coli was most prevalent in general stables and yards (37.7%) and offices (25.7%). Enterobacter spp. was the main organism in the environmental samples from ICU (24.2%) and isolation unit (22.9%, along with E. coli). Concerningly, hand-plate sampling showed that MRSA was the most common organism detected on hands (8.4%), followed by A. baumannii (5.2%) and E. cloacae (3.9%); however, E. coli, P. aeruginosa and K. pneumoniae were not found in these samples. Inconsistent sampling limited longitudinal analysis. We generated baseline environmental contamination data and demonstrated high E. coli-SKAPE hospital surface and hand contamination, informing infection control to prevent environment-to-patient cross-transmission.

title: Structural characterization of isomeric saponins by integrating diagnostic mass fragmentation and chromatographic retention rules: A case study of horse chestnut saponins-aescins.
abstract: The widespread presence of positional isomers, functional group isomers, and enantiomeric isomers in natural medicines poses a significant analytical challenge. Owing to their highly similar mass spectrometric fragmentation pathways, traditional liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) structural analysis techniques frequently struggle to distinguish the specific functional groups and substitution position of the groups in isomers, thus complicating the natural product characterization. The active principle of sodium aescinate for injection is a mixture composed of four primary isomeric saponins and isomeric impurities, necessitating advanced analytical strategies to resolve these constitutional isomers. In this study, the structures of nine laboratory-prepared impurities were fully structurally elucidated; their equilibrium isomeric mixtures were harvested for downstream studies.
